lesson.menu_title: Executive Communication -- Bad News, Balanced: Reporting a Setback to the Committee
lesson.menu_desc: The cost overrun goes to the steering committee. Read how executives report bad news upward, then balance the problem and the plan with contrast linkers -- "Although we are over budget, the go-live date has not changed", "Despite the setback, the risk is under control"
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 24 -- Executive Communication -- Bad News, Balanced: Reporting a Setback to the Committee
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Carlos Vinicius Vale Bassan | Lesson 24 -- Bad News, Balanced
lesson.grammar_point: contrast and concession linkers (although, even though, despite + noun / -ing, however)

listenings.text: When you report bad news to a committee, your first minute decides everything. Here are three rules. First, lead with the number. Do not downplay it, and do not hide it on the last slide. Say it clearly: we are two hundred thousand dollars over budget. Second, explain the root cause in one sentence, and do not blame another team. Even though the problem may not be yours, you are accountable for the solution. Third, balance the bad news with a plan. This is where small words like although and despite help you. For example: although we are over budget, the go-live date has not changed. Or: despite the setback, the risk is under control. One sentence like that tells the committee two things: you are honest, and you are in control. Remember, committees forgive problems. They do not forgive surprises.

Good morning, everyone. I will start with the difficult part. The payroll bridge is two hundred thousand dollars over budget, which is about eight percent. The root cause was testing. We found errors in the old payroll data, and we needed three extra weeks of tests to fix them. Although this was not in the original plan, I believe it was the right decision, because the alternative was paying people the wrong salaries. Here is how we will mitigate the impact. We will use one hundred and twenty thousand dollars from the contingency budget, and savings in the travel budget will offset another fifty thousand. Despite the extra cost, the go-live date of March first has not changed. Carlos and I are happy to take your questions.

reading.rtitle: How to Report Bad News Upward
paras: Every project has setbacks. What matters is how they are reported. When a cost overrun appears, many managers are tempted to downplay it: they put the number on slide twelve, or they call it a small adjustment. Although this feels safer at the time, it usually backfires. The committee finds out anyway, and when it does, it stops trusting the next report.

Experienced executives do the opposite. They are transparent from the first minute: the number comes first. Then they explain the root cause in one or two sentences, without blaming anyone. Even though the cause may be another team, the person who presents stays accountable for the solution. Finally, they show how they will mitigate the impact: money from the contingency budget, a smaller scope, or savings in another area that offset the extra cost.

The secret is balance. Despite the bad news, the update should not sound like a disaster; however, it should not sound like nothing happened, either. A good update says, in one breath, that the project is over budget and that the risk is under control. Bad news reported early is a problem. Bad news discovered late is a crisis.
